extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, exercises, and proofs describing intersection products, ampleness criteria, and related tools (Riemann–Roch, projection formula, Grothendieck group) for projective/proper varieties, especially surfaces. Includes concrete examples (P1×P1, blow-ups, Hirzebruch surfaces) and structural results (Nakai–Moishezon, Hodge index, c1 action on K-theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multilinearity of the intersection product
rubrics_metrics.description: The intersection product (L1 · L2 · ... · Ln · F) is multilinear in each invertible sheaf Li; in particular it is linear in each Li separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by writing line bundles as differences of very ample bundles (Exercise 16.2.F) and using vanishing results (Exercise 18.6.A and symmetry). The text shows linearity by substituting very ample bundles and using expressions such as (20.1.3.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing for too many factors (dim Supp F condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is projective and dim Supp F < n+1, then the intersection product of n+1 invertible sheaves with a coherent sheaf F vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as Exercise 20.1.H. The result also holds with 'projective' replaced by 'proper' because the underlying results extend to that setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical invariance of the intersection product
rubrics_metrics.description: On a projective scheme X, the intersection product depends only on the numerical equivalence classes of the Li.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 20.1.4. The proof uses that every line bundle may be written as the difference of two very ample line bundles (Exercise 16.2.F) and an induction on the number of factors; the proper case is handled by references ([FGIKNV, Prop. B.20]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic Riemann–Roch (polynomiality and leading coefficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is projective, F a coherent sheaf with dim Supp F = n, and L a line bundle on X, then χ(X, L^{⊗m} ⊗ F) is a polynomial in m of degree at most n; the coefficient of m^n is (L^n · F)/n!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 20.1.I. Hint: use vanishing of (L^{n+1} · F) from Exercise 20.1.H and expand via (20.1.1.1), mirroring the proof of polynomiality of the Hilbert polynomial (Theorem 18.6.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection formula for degree
rubrics_metrics.description: For a (projective) morphism π: X1 → X2 of integral projective varieties of the same dimension n, and invertible sheaves L1,...,Ln on X2, (π^*L1 · ... · π^*Ln) = deg(X1/X2)·(L1 · ... · Ln).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 20.1.J. Proof sketch: reduce by multilinearity to very ample Li, choose sections whose intersections lie in an open subset where π has genuine degree d, and use Chevalley's theorem and flatness/finite loci arguments (Exercises 10.3.G and 14.3.F). Handle the non-dominant case separately (degree convention d=0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized projection formula (pushforward/pullback interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: For π: X1 → X2 a morphism of proper varieties and F a coherent sheaf on X1 with dim Supp F ≤ n, and invertible sheaves L1,...,Ln on X2, one has (π_*L1 · ... · π_*Ln · π_*F) = (L1 · ... · Ln · F) (suitably interpreted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as 20.1.6 Remark: this generalizes Exercise 20.1.J; proofs are referenced in [FGIKNV, B.15] and [Ko1, Prop. VI.2.11]. The statement is phrased as a projection formula relating pushforwards and intersection products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive intersection for ample bundles on subvarieties
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is projective and L is an ample line bundle, then for any subvariety Y ⊂ X of dimension n, (L^n · Y) > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 20.1.K. Hint: reduce to very ample case and identify (L^n · Y) with deg Y in the projective embedding given by |L|. This fact is one direction of Nakai–Moishezon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nakai–Moishezon criterion for ampleness
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is an invertible sheaf on a projective k-scheme X and for every irreducible subvariety Y of X one has (L^{dim Y} · Y) > 0, then L is ample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 20.4.1. Remarks: 'projective' can be weakened to 'proper'. Proof uses induction on dimension, Asymptotic Riemann–Roch to show H^0 grows, writing L as difference of very ample bundles (Exercise 16.2.C), and Serre vanishing; the argument is carried out in multiple steps (20.4.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness of the ample cone
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of ample classes (ample cone) in N1_Q(X) is an open cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 20.4.3 / proof in 20.4.4: choose a basis of N1_Q, represent A as very ample after tensoring, and show small rational perturbations A + ε_i L_i remain ample (use that ample Q-line bundles form a cone and exercise 16.2.E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four equivalent descriptions of intersection number on a surface
rubrics_metrics.description: For effective divisors C and D on a regular projective surface X, the intersection number can be described by (20.2.0.1) deg_C OX(D)|C, (20.2.0.2) Euler characteristic formulation, (20.2.0.3) symmetry relation, and (20.2.0.4) scheme-theoretic intersection length h^0(C ∩ D, O_{C∩D}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise/Definition 20.2.A explains the equivalences and notes advantages/disadvantages: Euler characteristic hides geometry, (20.2.0.1) not obviously symmetric, (20.2.0.4) is local and interprets intersection multiplicity as length (example y−x^2 meets x-axis with multiplicity 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection pairing on Picard group and quadraticity of χ
rubrics_metrics.description: The intersection number induces a bilinear intersection form Pic X × Pic X → Z. For a divisor D on a surface, χ(X, O(nD)) is a quadratic polynomial in n whose coefficients relate to intersection numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Displayed as (20.2.4.1) and noted after Exercise 20.2.A; applies Asymptotic Riemann–Roch to identify coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-intersection equals degree of normal bundle
rubrics_metrics.description: For a curve C on a surface X, the self-intersection C·C equals the degree of the normal bundle to C in X (deg_C OX(C)|_C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark 20.2.2 references definition of normal bundle and equality of both viewpoints for self-intersection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of (−1)-curve
rubrics_metrics.description: A curve C ⊂ X that is isomorphic to P^1_k, consisting of smooth points, and with self-intersection C·C = −1 is called a (−1)-curve (equivalently, normal bundle O(−1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 20.2.8 and Exercise references (e.g., exceptional divisors of blow-ups have self-intersection −1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of intersection forms in key examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute intersection matrices and Picard groups for explicit surfaces: P^1×P^1 (Pic ≅ Zℓ ⊕ Zm with ℓ·m = 1), blow-up Bl_p P^2 (Pic generated by ℓ and e with ℓ·ℓ=1, e·e=−1, ℓ·e=0), and Hirzebruch surfaces F_n (Pic generated by E and F with explicit intersection pairings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 20.2.C, 20.2.D, 20.2.J–20.2.N guide concrete computations; hints point to use of scheme-theoretic preimages, proper transforms, and local charts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nef and effective cone descriptions for examples
rubrics_metrics.description: For Bl_p P^2 the nef cone is generated by ℓ and m (Exercise 20.2.F). On Hirzebruch surfaces F_n, the effective cone is generated by E and F and the nef cone by C and F (Exercises 20.2.P, 20.2.S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints: show boundary classes are nef by intersecting with generating curves, use moving families of curves and properties of linear series (Exercises 20.2.O,P). The cones' boundaries correspond to contractions/interesting morphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hodge Index Theorem (surface form)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is an irreducible smooth projective surface and H is ample with L·H = 0, then (a) L^2 ≤ 0, and (b) equality holds iff L is numerically trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 20.2.12. Proof uses Serre duality, Riemann–Roch for surfaces, vanishing of h^2 for sufficiently positive twists, and reduction to existence of effective divisors for large multiples (Exercises 20.2.B, 20.2.13–20.2.16). Generalizations relax smoothness; references given ([FGIKNV, Thm. B.27]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grothendieck group K(X) and its basic operations
rubrics_metrics.description: K(X) (often K_0(X)) is the abelian group generated by [F] for coherent sheaves F with relations [F]=[F'] if isomorphic and [F]=[F']+[F''] for short exact sequences. For proper X the Euler characteristic χ descends to K(X); for integral X rank descends to K(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 20.3.1. Emphasizes K(X) is universal for additive behavior on exact sequences and cautions about notation conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensional filtration on K(X) and A'_d(X)
rubrics_metrics.description: K(X) has a filtration by dimension of support: K(X)_{≤d} generated by coherent sheaves supported in dimension ≤ d. The graded piece A'_d(X) := K(X)_{≤d} / K(X)_{≤d−1} plays the role of homology; classes [Y] = [O_Y] for d-dimensional subvarieties lie in A'_d(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 20.3.2; this is called the coniveau or dimensional filtration. Many functorial properties (pushforward, flat pullback) respect this filtration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action of line bundles (first Chern class) on K(X)/A'•
rubrics_metrics.description: For a line bundle L, define an operator on K(X) by L ∩ [F] = [L⊗F] − [F], which sends K(X)_{≤d} to K(X)_{≤d−1} and descends to c1(L) ∩ : A'_d(X) → A'_{d−1}(X). On the associated graded (A'•) this action is additive in L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 20.3.A and 20.3.B explain why the operator is well-defined and additive on the graded pieces; this recovers the intersection product via repeated c1 actions: (L1·...·Ln·F) = c1(L1)∩...∩c1(Ln)∩[F].

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality of K-theory and relation to intersection (pushforward formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a proper morphism π: X1 → X2, pushforward on K-theory is given on classes by [π_*F] = Σ (−1)^i [R^i π_* F]; this descends to maps on A'_d which interact with c1 operations via a projection formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Displayed in (20.3.4.1). For flat morphisms π_* is exact and yields pullbacks on K-theory. The projection formula and compatibility with first Chern classes are emphasized; this is used to reprove projection formula results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between A'_d(X) and Chow groups Ad(X)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural surjection Ad(X) → A'_d(X); after tensoring with Q this is an isomorphism. The kernel is torsion in examples (e.g., exceptional torsion in group E8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equation (20.3.4.2) and subsequent remarks: references [F2] and [SGA6, Exp. XIV] for subtleties; kernel phenomena (2-,3-,5-torsion) are noted for special groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for proving ampleness via sections and vanishing
rubrics_metrics.description: To show L is ample under Nakai–Moishezon hypotheses: (i) use Asymptotic Riemann–Roch to show χ(X,L^{⊗m}) grows and hence H^0 eventually nonzero; (ii) write L as difference of very ample bundles and use exact sequences to control higher cohomology; (iii) use induction on dimension and Serre vanishing to produce global generation off an effective divisor, then kill base locus inductively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlined in Steps 1–3 of 20.4.5: write L ≅ A ⊗ B^{−1} with A,B very ample, use sequences (20.4.5.1)-(20.4.5.3), Serre vanishing, and inductive hypothesis that L|_D is ample to show global generation for high multiples.
